opus-5.5.text:
I think it comes down to what an agent actually does all day. In a chat setting, the model reads a question and writes an answer, and you're done. An agent is different. It runs in a loop: it calls a tool, reads the result, thinks, calls another tool, and it might do that dozens or hundreds of times on one task. So the context keeps growing, and the model is constantly re-reading a huge history and generating a lot of tokens.

When we designed the architecture, we were thinking about that pattern very directly. Three things matter most.

**Long context has to be cheap.** If attention cost explodes as the trajectory gets longer, the agent becomes slow and expensive right when the task gets interesting. So we put a lot of effort into making long-context inference efficient. Not just supporting a long window on paper, but keeping memory and compute manageable when you're actually sitting at very long lengths for a long time.

**Decoding speed matters more than people think.** Agents generate a lot: reasoning, tool calls, code. If each step is slow, the whole loop is slow, and you can't afford to explore or retry. A sparse, efficient design lets you keep a large total capacity while only activating part of it per token. That gives you a better tradeoff between intelligence and throughput, and in agent scenarios throughput directly becomes capability, because you can try more things within the same budget.

**Architecture and training have to be co-designed.** Agentic ability really comes from reinforcement learning on long, multi-step environments. That RL is extremely rollout-heavy. If your inference is efficient, you can run far more rollouts, longer trajectories, and more environments, and the model simply learns more. So an efficient architecture isn't just a deployment advantage. It feeds back into how good the model becomes during training.

So I wouldn't say there's one magic trick. It's more that we stopped treating the architecture as something fixed and asked, "If the main workload is long-horizon agents, what should the model look like?" Once you take that question seriously, a lot of design decisions follow naturally.

r002.rationale: The response says long-context memory should remain manageable, but does not state that a smaller KV cache enables caching for more agent instances.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd push back a little on the framing first: I don't think architecture alone makes a model good at agents. What makes a model good at agents is whether it can keep its judgment stable across a very long, messy sequence of actions. The architecture matters because it decides how cheaply you can give the model that long sequence, and how much of it the model can actually use.

Let me break that into three things.

The first is context cost. An agent doesn't answer a question once. It reads a file, runs a command, gets an error, reads the error, tries again. A real coding task can run to hundreds of thousands of tokens before it's done. If your attention cost scales badly with sequence length, the agent gets slower and more expensive with every step, and in practice people just cut the loop short. The work we did on compressing the KV cache, on multi-head latent attention, started as a memory problem. But the consequence for agents is that you can afford to let the model keep everything it has seen. It doesn't have to forget step three by step forty.

The second is sparsity. With a mixture-of-experts design, you activate a small fraction of parameters per token. People usually describe that as a training efficiency trick, and it is. But think about what an agent's token stream looks like: a bit of natural language reasoning, then a tool call, then a huge dump of structured output, then reasoning again. Those are very different distributions of tokens. Having experts that specialize means the model isn't forcing one dense set of weights to be equally good at parsing a stack trace and planning the next move. Routing lets the compute go where the token needs it.

The third is inference economics, which people underrate. Agents are mostly a decoding problem. You are generating lots of tokens, with lots of round trips to tools in between. If each decoded token is expensive, your agent is a demo and not a product. Multi-token prediction, a small active parameter count, a compact cache. These don't make any single answer smarter. They make it possible to run the model long enough to finish the job. And when you can run more rollouts cheaply, your reinforcement learning on agent tasks also gets better, because you can collect many more full trajectories per unit of compute. So architecture feeds back into training, not only serving.

One honest caveat. Everything I just said is about capacity and cost. The thing that actually makes an agent reliable is post-training: learning when to verify, when to stop, when to say the task can't be done. The architecture only buys you the room to learn that. If you train poorly, a very efficient model will just make mistakes faster and cheaper.

r002.rationale: It says a compact cache helps the model retain more of its context, but does not explain that a smaller KV cache allows caching for more agent instances.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is that an agent needs more than a good answer to a single question. It needs to take an action, observe what happens, and then decide what to do next. That means the model has to maintain context and stay reliable across many steps.

So I would look at the architecture in terms of how efficiently it supports that loop. Can it handle a growing context? Can it reason carefully when a decision is difficult without making every step expensive? Those properties matter because an agent may call the model many times to complete one task.

But I wouldn’t attribute agent capability to architecture alone. Training, tool use, and the environment all matter. The architecture gives you a foundation; the real test is whether the whole system can complete a task and recover when something goes wrong.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is that an agent doesn’t just answer a question once. It has to act, observe what happened, and then decide what to do next. That means the model needs to maintain the relevant context across many steps, reason about feedback, and use tools reliably.

So when I think about an architecture for agents, I’m looking at both capability and efficiency. Can it support that repeated loop without becoming too expensive? Can it keep track of the goal as the context grows? Those are the properties that make an architecture useful for agents. But architecture alone isn’t enough—the training and the environment you put the model in matter just as much.
